message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"6.1","text":"On the third day, when I had come with my closest companions to the appointed place in Tyre, I found Appion seated between Annubion and Athenodorus, waiting for us together with many other men of learning. Even so, without being at all daunted, I greeted them and sat down opposite Appion. Before long he began to speak: “I want to begin first from this point and so come quickly now to the matter under inquiry. Before you were here with us, my child Clement, this Annubion and Athenodorus—who yesterday, along with the others, listened to you as you engaged in discussion—recounted to me how, when I associated with you in Rome, when you were supposedly in love, I told you many lies about the gods, saying that they were lovers of boys, licentious, mating with mothers, sisters, and daughters, and implicated in countless adulteries. But you should have known, my child, that I did not write such things because I thought this way about the gods. Rather, out of affection for you, I held back from telling the truth. If you want those truths now, hear them from me.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"σὺν τοῖς οἰκειοτάτοις","chosen":"with my closest companions","rationale":"The superlative denotes those most intimately associated with Clement, not merely members of a household."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ἐκ παιδείας ἀνδρῶν","chosen":"men of learning","rationale":"The phrase identifies men distinguished by education or cultivated learning."},{"source_quote":"συνερχόμενός σοι ὡς ἐρῶντι","chosen":"when I associated with you in Rome, when you were supposedly in love","rationale":"The dative participle ἐρῶντι most naturally agrees with σοι and characterizes Clement; alternatives such as “as though you were a lover” convey the same basic attachment."},{"source_quote":"πολλὰ τῶν θεῶν κατεψευσάμην","chosen":"I told you many lies about the gods","rationale":"The middle verb with the genitive means to speak falsely about someone; “slandered the gods extensively” is a possible stronger alternative."},{"source_quote":"τὰ ἀληθῆ λέγειν ἀπεκρυπτόμην","chosen":"I held back from telling the truth","rationale":"The middle verb expresses Appion’s concealing or withholding himself from truthful disclosure; “kept the truth concealed” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.2","text":"The wisest among the men of ancient times, though they themselves had learned the whole truth through toil, kept the unworthy and those who did not aspire to divine instruction from receiving the knowledge. For neither were twelve children born from Uranus and his mother Earth—as the myth enumerates them, the males being Oceanus, Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, Iapetus, and Cronus, and the females Theia, Themis, Mnemosyne, Demeter, Tethys, and Rhea—nor did Cronus cut off the genitals of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle, as you say, and throw them into the deep. Nor did Aphrodite come into being from drops of blood flowing from the mutilation of Uranus. Nor, again, did Cronus mate with Rhea, father Pluto first, and swallow him because he feared, on account of a certain decree of Prometheus, that a child born from him might become nobler than he and deprive him of his kingdom. He did not father Poseidon second and swallow him in the same way. Nor, after these, when Zeus was born, did his mother Rhea hide him and, when Cronus demanded something to swallow, give him a stone instead. That stone, though not swallowed, compressed those swallowed earlier and drove them out, so that the first to emerge was Pluto, the first swallowed, after him Poseidon, and Zeus third. Nor indeed, as they say, was Zeus preserved through his mother’s foresight and, after ascending into heaven, did he remove his father from the kingdom. He did not punish his father’s brothers. He did not descend out of desire for mortal women. He did not shamefully have intercourse with sisters or daughters, with his brothers’ wives, or with boys. Nor, after fathering Metis, did he swallow her ...., so as to make Athena spring from his brain out of Metis and give birth to Dionysus from his thigh, whom they say was torn limb from limb by the Titans. No feast took place at the marriage of Thetis and Peleus. He did not exclude Eris from the wedding. Eris, after being dishonored, did not devise conflict and dissension among the banqueters. She did not take a golden apple from the gardens of the Hesperides and inscribe on it, “A gift for the beautiful one.” Next they tell the story that Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite find the apple and, as they quarrel over it, go to Zeus. He does not judge between them himself but sends them by Hermes to the shepherd Paris to be judged concerning their beauty. But neither were the goddesses judged nor did Paris award the apple to Aphrodite. After being honored, Aphrodite did not honor him in return with marriage to Helen. For the honor paid to the goddess would not have become the occasion for a war involving every people, and that to the destruction of the man who had received the honor and was closely related to Aphrodite’s family. Rather, as I said, my child, such stories possess a proper and philosophical explanation that can be expressed through allegory, so that when you hear it you will marvel.” And I said, “Please do not torture me by delaying.” He replied, “Do not be afraid. I will not postpone it, but will begin speaking now.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀπεκρύψαντο τὴν ἐπιστήμην λαβεῖν","chosen":"kept the unworthy and those who did not aspire to divine instruction from receiving the knowledge","rationale":"The construction presents the sages as withholding access to knowledge. A more formally literal alternative is “concealed from them the receiving of knowledge.”"},{"source_quote":"τῇ ἐξ ἀδάμαντος ἅρπῃ","chosen":"with an adamantine sickle","rationale":"Ἅρπη denotes a curved cutting implement, while ἀδάμας identifies its proverbial unyielding material; “adamant sickle” is a closer but less natural alternative."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τινὰ Προμηθέως θεσμὸν","chosen":"on account of a certain decree of Prometheus","rationale":"Θεσμός may denote an ordinance, pronouncement, or established decree. “Prediction of Prometheus” would fit the mythic context but is less direct lexically."},{"source_quote":"ὃς οὐ καταποθεὶς τοὺς προκαταποθέντας θλίψας ἐξῶσεν","chosen":"That stone, though not swallowed, compressed those swallowed earlier and drove them out","rationale":"The translation retains the printed negation οὐ and the stone as the grammatical subject, despite the resulting departure from the familiar myth."},{"source_quote":"οὐ παισὶν αἰσχρῶς συνεγένετο","chosen":"He did not shamefully have intercourse with boys","rationale":"Παῖδες can mean children or boys; the earlier accusation that the gods were παιδεράστας supports “boys” here."},{"source_quote":"οὐδὲ Μῆτιν γεννήσας κατέπιεν","chosen":"Nor, after fathering Metis, did he swallow her","rationale":"Μῆτιν can be construed with γεννήσας and then understood as the object of κατέπιεν. An alternative is “Nor, after begetting offspring, did he swallow Metis,” but the printed gap prevents certainty about the larger construction."},{"source_quote":"δῶρον τῇ καλῇ","chosen":"A gift for the beautiful one","rationale":"The Greek has the positive adjective “beautiful,” not an explicit superlative such as “the fairest.”"},{"source_quote":"παμφύλου πολέμου","chosen":"a war involving every people","rationale":"The adjective describes a war encompassing all tribes or peoples; “a universal war” is a concise alternative."},{"source_quote":"ἔχει τινὰ λόγον τὰ τοιαῦτα οἰκεῖον καὶ φιλόσοφον","chosen":"such stories possess a proper and philosophical explanation","rationale":"Λόγος here is an explanatory account, while οἰκεῖος can mean proper, fitting, or inherent."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὃς οὐ καταποθεὶς τοὺς προκαταποθέντας θλίψας ἐξῶσεν","issue":"The supplied reading explicitly says that the stone was not swallowed, yet makes it compress and expel those previously swallowed. This is internally incongruous and differs from the familiar myth, but it remains grammatically translatable and has therefore not been corrected.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"οὐδὲ Μῆτιν γεννήσας κατέπιεν ...., ἵνα","issue":"The four printed points mark a visible gap after κατέπιεν. The omitted wording cannot be restored from the supplied source, and the gap may affect both the Metis construction and the following purpose clause.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"6.3","text":"There was once a time when nothing existed except chaos and an undifferentiated mixture of elements still heaped together in disorder, as nature itself acknowledges and the great men have understood to be the case. As a witness from among those great in wisdom I will present to you the greatest, Homer himself, who said concerning the confusion from the beginning, “But may you all become water and earth,” thereby indicating that all things had their origin from those and that, after the dissolution of their moist and earthy substance, they are restored again to the first nature, which is chaos. Hesiod says in the Theogony, “Indeed, first of all, Chaos came to be.” The words “came to be” clearly signify having come into being, as generated things do, not existing always, as ungenerated things do. Orpheus also likens chaos to an egg, in which was the confusion of the first elements. Hesiod posits this as chaos, but Orpheus calls it a generated egg, projected from infinite matter and brought into being as follows:","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"στοιχείων ἀτάκτων ἔτι συντεφορημένων μίξις ἀδιάκριτος","chosen":"an undifferentiated mixture of elements still heaped together in disorder","rationale":"Ἀδιάκριτος emphasizes that the elements had not been separated, while συντεφορημένων pictures them as swept or heaped together."},{"source_quote":"περὶ τῆς ἀνέκαθεν συγχύσεως","chosen":"concerning the confusion from the beginning","rationale":"Ἀνέκαθεν may mean from above or from the beginning; the cosmogonic context supports the temporal sense."},{"source_quote":"ἀλλὰ ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα γένοισθε","chosen":"But may you all become water and earth","rationale":"The wording is translated directly as quoted here rather than conformed to a familiar English rendering of Homer."},{"source_quote":"ὡς γενητὰ ... ὡς ἀγένητα","chosen":"as generated things do ... as ungenerated things do","rationale":"The paired adjectives contrast things that come into being with things that do not originate; “created” and “uncreated” could introduce a stronger theological nuance than the immediate argument requires."},{"source_quote":"ἐξ ἀπείρου τῆς ὕλης προβεβλημένον","chosen":"projected from infinite matter","rationale":"Προβάλλω depicts the egg as put or cast forth from matter; “emanated from” is a possible philosophical alternative."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.4","text":"Since fourfold matter was animate, and since a certain entirely infinite abyss was always flowing, being carried along without distinction, bringing up countless incomplete mixtures, one after another, and therefore dissolving them through its disorder, and since it gaped open so that it could not be bound together for the generation of a living creature, it happened at one time, as the infinite sea itself was being driven around by its own nature, that by a natural motion it flowed in an orderly fashion from the same point to the same point like a whirlpool and mixed the substances. And thus, from what is heard, the choicest part of all things—that which was most suitable for the generation of a living creature—flowed as in a funnel through the middle of the whole, made its way into the depth under the force of the whirlpool that carried everything, drew in the surrounding spirit, and, having been gathered as into something most fertile, formed a structure capable of differentiation. For just as a bubble tends to form in liquid, so a spherical vessel was formed, enclosed on every side. Afterward, once it had gestated within itself and was borne upward by the divine spirit it had taken in, this very great offspring came forth into the light, as an animate created work born from the entire infinite abyss, resembling the roundness of eggs and swift in its flight.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τῆς τετραγενοῦς ὕλης ἐμψύχου οὔσης","chosen":"Since fourfold matter was animate","rationale":"Τετραγενής describes matter as constituted in four kinds, presumably the four elements, while ἔμψυχος presents it as animate or ensouled."},{"source_quote":"μυρίας ἀτελεῖς κράσεις ἄλλοτε ἄλλας ἐπαναγέοντος","chosen":"bringing up countless incomplete mixtures, one after another","rationale":"The abyss repeatedly produces or brings up mixtures that never reach completion."},{"source_quote":"κινήσει φυσικῇ εὐτάκτως ῥυῆναι ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ ὥσπερ ἴλιγγα","chosen":"by a natural motion it flowed in an orderly fashion from the same point to the same point like a whirlpool","rationale":"The repeated “same” describes recurrent or circular motion; “from the same place back to the same place” is an explanatory alternative."},{"source_quote":"τὸ νοστιμώτατον","chosen":"the choicest part","rationale":"The superlative can suggest what is most pleasant, excellent, or productive. The following clause identifies it as the portion best suited to producing life."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ τῆς πάντα φερούσης ἴλιγγος","chosen":"under the force of the whirlpool that carried everything","rationale":"The participle portrays the vortex as bearing all things along; “all-bearing whirlpool” would preserve the compact form less idiomatically."},{"source_quote":"ὡς εἰς γονιμώτατον συλληφθὲν","chosen":"having been gathered as into something most fertile","rationale":"The neuter superlative lacks an expressed noun. It may refer to a fertile place, receptacle, or mass, so the English retains the indefinite comparison."},{"source_quote":"ποιεῖν κριτικὴν σύστασιν","chosen":"formed a structure capable of differentiation","rationale":"Κριτικός here likely concerns separation or discrimination among the mixed constituents; “a differentiating composition” is a more compact alternative."},{"source_quote":"σφαιροειδὲς πανταχόθεν συνελήφθη κύτος","chosen":"a spherical vessel was formed, enclosed on every side","rationale":"Κύτος denotes a hollow body, cavity, or containing vessel, fitting the developing cosmic egg."},{"source_quote":"τῇ περιφερείᾳ τῶν ὠῶν προσεοικὸς καὶ τῷ τάχει τῆς πτήσεως","chosen":"resembling the roundness of eggs and swift in its flight","rationale":"The first dative supplies the comparison with eggs, while the second describes speed of flight. A formally stricter “resembling the roundness of eggs and the speed of flight” is possible but awkward and semantically unclear."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐξ ἀκουστοῦ","issue":"In this context the printed phrase, ordinarily meaning “from what is heard” or “from report,” has no clear semantic relationship to the formation of the life-producing portion. No contextually secure English sense or supported correction can be established from the supplied reading.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true},{"source_quote":"τῇ περιφερείᾳ τῶν ὠῶν προσεοικὸς καὶ τῷ τάχει τῆς πτήσεως","issue":"The coordination clearly mentions both resemblance to the roundness of eggs and speed of flight, but the precise syntactic relation of the second dative to προσεοικὸς is uncertain. The main rendering preserves both claims without supplying an unexpressed comparison object.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.5","text":"Understand Cronus, then, as time, and Rhea as the flow of moist substance, because all matter, carried along in time, brought forth the spherical heaven that contains everything, like an egg. At first it was full of generative marrow, as though able to bring forth elements and colors of every kind; and yet from one substance and one color it bore an appearance of every kind. For just as in a peacock’s egg the egg’s color appears to be one, but potentially it contains within itself countless colors of what is destined to reach maturity, so also the animate egg born from infinite matter, set in motion by the underlying and ever-flowing matter, displays transformations of every kind. For within its circumference an androgynous living creature takes form through the providence of the divine spirit present within it. Orpheus calls him Phanes, because when he appeared, the whole shone out from him through the radiance of fire—the most brilliant of the elements—which was brought to maturity in moisture. And this is not incredible, because in the case of glowworms too, nature has granted us, as a demonstration, to see moist light.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Κρόνον οὖν τὸν χρόνον μοι νόει","chosen":"Understand Cronus, then, as time","rationale":"The interpretation depends on the sound association between Κρόνος and χρόνος; the English states the allegorical identification directly."},{"source_quote":"τὴν δὲ Ῥέαν τὸ ῥέον τῆς ὑγρᾶς οὐσίας","chosen":"and Rhea as the flow of moist substance","rationale":"The author connects the name Rhea with the participle ῥέον, “flowing.”"},{"source_quote":"τοῦ γονίμου μυελοῦ","chosen":"generative marrow","rationale":"The phrase describes an interior substance capable of producing differentiated elements and colors; “fertile marrow” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"παντοδαπὴν ἐκ μιᾶς οὐσίας τε καὶ χρώματος ἑνὸς ἔφερε τὴν φαντασίαν","chosen":"from one substance and one color it bore an appearance of every kind","rationale":"The translation retains the explicit contrast between manifold appearance and a single substance and color rather than smoothing it into uniform appearance."},{"source_quote":"ἐν τῷ τοῦ ταῶ γεννήματι","chosen":"in a peacock’s egg","rationale":"Literally “in the product or offspring of the peacock”; the immediate reference to the egg’s color identifies the intended object."},{"source_quote":"παντοδαπὰς ἐκφαίνει τροπάς","chosen":"displays transformations of every kind","rationale":"Τροπαί are changes, turnings, or transformations manifested as the egg develops."},{"source_quote":"ζῷόν τι ἀρρενόθηλυ εἰδοποιεῖται","chosen":"an androgynous living creature takes form","rationale":"Ἀρρενόθηλυ combines male and female, while εἰδοποιεῖται describes acquisition of determinate form."},{"source_quote":"ὃν Φάνητα Ὀρφεὺς καλεῖ","chosen":"Orpheus calls him Phanes","rationale":"The masculine relative pronoun shifts from the grammatically neuter ζῷον to the personified being Phanes."},{"source_quote":"τῷ φέγγει τοῦ διαπρεπεστάτου τῶν στοιχείων πυρὸς","chosen":"through the radiance of fire—the most brilliant of the elements","rationale":"The superlative identifies fire as preeminent in brilliance among the elements."},{"source_quote":"ὑγρὸν φῶς","chosen":"moist light","rationale":"The unusual phrase is retained directly because it supports the preceding claim that fire or light reaches maturity in moisture; “light in moisture” is a possible interpretive alternative."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
